title: GeoJSON Formatter: Pretty-Print for Humans
description: Format minified or messy GeoJSON into clean, readable, indented JSON with the GeoJSON Formatter — locally in your browser. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a one-line 669-byte sample file unfolds into 88 readable lines — same data, same coordinates, but finally a document a human can review, diff and debug.
quick_answer: The GeoJSON Formatter formats minified or messy GeoJSON into clean, consistently indented JSON — locally in your browser, without uploading the file. Paste the tangle and read the structure: features, geometries and properties laid out line by line, exactly as valid as before and infinitely easier to work with.

The endpoint returned something odd. Formatted, the oddity has a line number and a neighbourhood; unformatted, it has a scroll bar.
Fixing one property or deleting one feature by hand demands visible structure. Format, edit, and (if the consumer prefers) re-minify.
Pasting a readable excerpt into a ticket gets answers; pasting a 40,000-character line gets silence.

body.t: A sample collection measures 1,521 bytes pretty and 669 minified — indentation is more than half the file. Formatting buys readability with bytes; minifying buys bytes with readability. Know which currency your moment needs.

popular_table.note: Formatting is lossless by definition — it re-lays the same JSON. If a formatter ever changed a number, it would be a bug, not a style choice.

faq: Yes — formatting runs locally in your browser. Once the page has loaded, no network is involved and the file never leaves your machine, which is why this page is safe for data you would not paste into a server-side tool.
Consistent two-space indentation, the JSON community’s house style — readable nesting without runaway width on deep geometry arrays.
Then the input is not valid JSON — the formatter’s parse error is your first debugging gift: it localises the breakage better than a blank map does.
JSON forbids them; JavaScript tolerates them. Files ‘almost JSON’ from JS literals need the commas stripped before any strict formatter can help.
Browser memory is the ceiling; ordinary datasets format instantly. Multi-hundred-megabyte files belong to streaming formatters (jq) applying the same idea.
Formatting preserves the file’s key order — deliberate, because GeoJSON writers’ ordering (type, geometry, properties) is a readability feature, not noise.
The numeric values are preserved; their textual dress (40.0 versus 40) may normalise through parse-and-print — the value is identical, the archaeology of its typing is not sacred.
